content: For individuals who are stable on ART with suppressed viral loads, less frequent clinical visits and longer medication supplies may be appropriate. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), stability on ART is defined as being on treatment for at least 12 months, having no adverse drug reactions requiring regular monitoring, no current illnesses, a good understanding of adherence, and evidence of treatment success (e.g. For individuals with advanced HIV disease, more intensive follow-up and a comprehensive package of interventions can help reduce morbidity and mortality. This group includes people newly diagnosed with HIV and those re-engaging in care after ART interruption. The 2016 WHO consolidated antiretroviral (ARV) guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for managing advanced HIV disease, particularly in resource-limited settings. Advanced HIV disease in adults and adolescents is defined as a CD4 cell count below 200 cells/mm³ or the presence of a WHO stage 3 or 4 clinical event. For children under five years of age, all are considered to have advanced HIV disease at presentation due to their heightened risk of disease progression and mortality. Despite the scale-up of ART in lowand middle-income countries, the proportion of people presenting with advanced HIV disease has remained largely unchanged over the past five years. Recent estimates suggest that 30–40% of individuals starting ART in these settings have CD4 counts below 200 cells/mm³, and 20% have CD4 counts below 100 cells/mm³. Many individuals with advanced HIV disease also return to care after ART interruption, often with low CD4 counts and clinical symptoms. The leading causes of mortality among adults with advanced HIV disease globally include tuberculosis (TB), severe bacterial infections, cryptococcal meningitis, toxoplasmosis, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP). In 2015, approximately 1 million people died from AIDS-related causes, with TB accounting for a significant proportion of these deaths. Young children living with HIV are particularly vulnerable to TB progression following initial infection. Severe bacterial infections, including bloodstream, respiratory, central nervous system, and gastrointestinal infections, are also common among individuals with advanced HIV disease, contributing to significant morbidity and mortality. Cryptococcal meningitis remains a major cause of mortality among hospitalized adults with HIV, accounting for 15–20% of adult deaths. The incidence of cryptococcal meningitis is highest in sub-Saharan Africa, with an estimated 223,100 cases globally in 2014. Pre-emptive therapy for asymptomatic individuals who test positive for cryptococcal antigen is a key strategy to prevent this condition. Similarly, PJP is a leading cause of mortality among hospitalized adults and children with HIV, though its global burden is poorly characterized due to limited diagnostic facilities. Toxoplasmosis, particularly cerebral toxoplasmosis, is a frequent cause of brain lesions in adults with HIV who are not receiving co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. The prevalence of toxoplasmosis co-infection is especially high in sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East. Diagnosis often requires imaging techniques, which are not widely available in resource-limited settings. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection, particularly CMV retinitis, is another significant concern among severely immunocompromised individuals, with the highest prevalence reported in Asia. The WHO guidelines recommend a package of care for individuals with advanced HIV disease, including screening, treatment, and/or prophylaxis for major opportunistic infections, rapid ART initiation, and intensified adherence support. Key interventions include co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, TB preventive treatment, cryptococcal antigen screening, and pre-emptive antifungal therapy for those with positive cryptococcal antigen results. Rapid ART initiation should be deferred in cases of suspected TB or cryptococcal meningitis to avoid life-threatening complications. Two randomized trials, REMSTART and REALITY, have demonstrated the effectiveness of enhanced care packages in reducing mortality among individuals with advanced HIV disease. These interventions include community support, enhanced TB screening, and prophylaxis for opportunistic infections. The REALITY trial, for example, showed a 28% reduction in mortality with an enhanced prophylaxis package, which included fluconazole, co-trimoxazole, isoniazid, azithromycin, and albendazole. The WHO emphasizes the importance of baseline CD4 testing to identify individuals with advanced HIV disease and guide clinical management. While routine viral load monitoring is recommended for ART response, CD4 testing remains critical for identifying severe immunosuppression. Adherence support, including tailored counseling and community-based follow-up, is essential for individuals with advanced HIV disease, who may face significant challenges in attending clinic appointments and managing complex treatment regimens. The package of care for advanced HIV disease requires initial investment but is cost-effective in reducing the burden of opportunistic infections, hospitalizations, and mortality. The WHO continues to refine its recommendations to address the needs of this vulnerable population, with a focus on evidence-based interventions and programmatic feasibility.
